title: Salesforce Release Cycle, Release Notes, Maintenance, and API Versions
objectives: Describe Salesforce's seasonal release rhythm and why admins must track it.
Use release notes to assess impact before upgrades hit production.
Explain maintenance windows vs feature releases.
Relate API versions to integrations and developer projects.
diagnostic_question: An integration breaks the week after a Salesforce release. The developer says 'we did not change our code.' What release-related factors do you check first?
definition: Salesforce delivers three major seasonal releases per year. A Salesforce Help upgrade FAQ states the seasonal releases occur in Spring (February), Summer (June), and Winter (October), that production upgrades cannot be delayed, and that sandbox preview is typically 4–5 weeks before production ([Salesforce upgrade release schedule FAQ](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=005224913)). Release notes document current behavior and feature availability ([Release notes](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=release-notes.salesforce_release_notes.htm)). In a REST URI, callers replace XX.X with the requested API version ([REST Resources and Requests](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_rest.meta/api_rest/intro_rest_resources.htm)); the [API End-of-Life Policy](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_rest.meta/api_rest/api_rest_eol.htm) records support, deprecation notices, and retirement status. Instance-specific dates remain Needs verification on Trust and the current release calendar.
why_it_matters: Shared platform upgrades mean your org changes even when your team ships nothing. Release literacy prevents surprise breakages in automation, integrations, and training materials.
sixty_second_explanation: Salesforce is a train on a schedule: Winter, Spring, Summer cars arrive for everyone on the line. Release notes are the passenger briefing. API version is which rulebook your integration carriage follows. Maintenance is scheduled track work.
deeper_explanation: A Salesforce Help upgrade FAQ states seasonal releases occur in Spring (February), Summer (June), and Winter (October), production upgrades cannot be delayed, and sandbox preview is typically 4–5 weeks before production. Instance-specific dates remain Needs verification ([Salesforce upgrade release schedule FAQ](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=005224913)).
[Release notes](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=release-notes.salesforce_release_notes.htm) are the authoritative feature and availability change catalog.
The same FAQ states Salesforce also applies maintenance releases automatically to sandboxes and production. Instance-specific windows remain Needs verification on the current Trust/status calendar.

REST callers select a version in the URI; use [REST Resources and Requests](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_rest.meta/api_rest/intro_rest_resources.htm) and the [API End-of-Life Policy](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_rest.meta/api_rest/api_rest_eol.htm) when planning version migration and testing.

mental_model.analogy: Seasonal city festival: platform upgrades the whole downtown on a calendar; vendors (your org) must read the bulletin (release notes) and test stalls (sandboxes) before opening night (prod impact).
where_it_breaks: The whole downtown upgrades—you cannot skip a seasonal release the way you skip a vendor stall.
Release notes may not list every edge case your integration hits.
Typical months (February/June/October) are FAQ guidance; your instance date is Needs verification on Trust and the current calendar.
Pinning an API version does not freeze Lightning UI or maintenance windows.

interview_questions.question: Describe the Salesforce seasonal release cycle and why admins must track it.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Salesforce ships three seasonal releases—Spring, Summer, and Winter. Help says typical months are February, June, and October, production upgrades cannot be delayed, and you must read release notes because the org changes even if your team ships nothing.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I start with the Help FAQ: three major releases per year, automatic production upgrades, and sandbox preview typically 4–5 weeks earlier. Instance dates are Needs verification on the current calendar. Release notes are the catalog of what changed. Maintenance releases are separate scheduled work. I tell interviewers I do not treat a release as optional and I do not invent exact hours. Preview testing is how we find Flow or integration breaks before production.
interview_questions.example: A Summer release changes a Flow action; the team that skipped release notes discovers it only after production users file tickets.
tradeoffs: Preview lead time versus the fact you cannot delay the production upgrade
follow_ups: How do you know if a sandbox is on preview?
What is the difference between a seasonal release and maintenance?
weak_answer_warnings: Says seasonal releases are optional or can be rolled back like a package

interview_questions.question: What is an API version, and how is it different from a seasonal release name?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: An API version is the numeric pin in a REST URI, such as v67.0. A seasonal release name like Summer '26 is the platform train. Pinning a version does not freeze Lightning UI or skip maintenance.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: REST documentation says callers replace XX.X in the URI with the version they want; the Versions resource lists what is available. The API End-of-Life Policy tracks support, deprecation, and retirement. I test a version bump in a sandbox first. I never confuse this with a managed-package version number. After a seasonal release, even an unchanged pin can see platform behavior changes, so release notes still matter.
interview_questions.example: An integration keeps calling /services/data/v61.0/ after Summer '26; you check EOL status and release notes before jumping to v67.0 in production.
tradeoffs: Stability of an old pin versus access to new fields on a newer API version
follow_ups: Where do you look up retirement status?
Does a pin freeze the UI?
weak_answer_warnings: Confuses API version with package version or release nickname

interview_questions.question: An executive asks why the integration broke when the team made no code changes.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: A seasonal release or maintenance window can change platform behavior without a local commit. I open release notes, check the API version, and reproduce in a preview sandbox before blaming the vendor.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: Unchanged application code is not proof the runtime is unchanged. Salesforce upgrades the shared platform on a calendar you cannot delay. I gather the error timestamp, the org's release, the REST version in the URI, and any overlapping Trust maintenance. Then I search release notes for the connector and Flow products we use. If preview is still available, I reproduce there. I do not recommend rolling back the Salesforce release—that is not a customer control.
interview_questions.example: The week after Summer production upgrades, a REST connector on v61.0 starts 400s; release notes list a related API behavior change the team never tested.
tradeoffs: Fast vendor blame versus evidence from notes, version, and preview
follow_ups: Was there a maintenance window the same night?
What API version is in the URI?
weak_answer_warnings: Blames users or says Salesforce never changes unless we deploy

interview_questions.question: The business wants a blackout-weekend go-live. What release and maintenance checks do you run first?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: I check the seasonal release calendar, whether sandboxes or production are in a preview or upgrade window, and Trust Status for a posted maintenance window on that instance.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: A go-live during a known maintenance window or the production upgrade weekend stacks two change events. Help says you cannot delay the seasonal production upgrade. I look up the instance, the next release or maintenance posting, and I ask to move the cutover if they overlap. I also confirm the API versions the cutover will call are still supported. Exact hours are Needs verification on the live status site—I do not invent them in the interview.
interview_questions.example: A marketing launch is booked the same Saturday Trust lists instance maintenance; you move the cutover rather than hope both succeed.
tradeoffs: Fixed marketing date versus availability risk from maintenance or a release
follow_ups: Which Salesforce instance is this org on?
Is a sandbox still on preview?
weak_answer_warnings: Ignores maintenance and release timing entirely

interview_questions.question: A feature appears in the release notes but users cannot see it. What do you check?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: I check whether the seasonal release actually reached this instance, then edition, permissions, and whether the notes say an admin must enable the feature.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: Release notes describe availability, not a guarantee every org sees every item. Some features require a click to enable; some are edition-gated—I mark gates as Needs verification rather than inventing SKUs. I confirm the org's current release in Setup, search the notes for enablement steps, and test in a preview sandbox if the production instance is not upgraded yet. I do not treat a missing feature as a broken API version unless the notes say so.
interview_questions.example: Summer notes mention a Setup toggle that is off by default; after the admin enables it in a preview sandbox, testers see the feature.
tradeoffs: Waiting for automatic on versus following documented enablement
follow_ups: Does the note say admin enablement is required?
weak_answer_warnings: Assumes the release notes item is a platform bug

interview_questions.question: An integration still calls an API version the End-of-Life Policy marks retired. What is your plan?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: I treat retirement as a deadline, pick a supported API version from the Versions resource, and test the migration in a sandbox before touching production.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: The API End-of-Life Policy documents support, deprecation notices, and retirement. I do not invent how many years remain—I open the current policy. Then I list callers, bump the URI version in a lower environment, run regression, and only then promote. A seasonal release can make retirement more urgent, but the pin and the release cycle are different levers. I also re-read release notes for the products those calls touch.
interview_questions.example: A nightly job still uses a retired REST version; you migrate it to v67.0 in a sandbox, compare payloads, then schedule the production URI change after sign-off.
tradeoffs: Staying on an old pin versus the cost of a tested version migration
follow_ups: What does the current EOL page say for that version?
weak_answer_warnings: Ignores support status or bumps the version only in production

interview_questions.question: Design a release-readiness process for a team with many integrations.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: I keep a matrix of owners, API versions, and products, then every seasonal release we filter release notes, run preview-sandbox regression, and sign off before production upgrades.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: The process has four beats: calendar, notes, preview, and version hygiene. Help gives the typical Spring/Summer/Winter months and says you cannot delay production. Owners filter release notes for their products. Preview sandboxes, when available, run automated and manual tests. The matrix records each integration's API version and EOL status. Maintenance windows are checked on Trust before go-lives. I do not promise a universal sandbox-preview entitlement for every org type.
interview_questions.example: A 50-integration shop tracks each REST URI version, assigns a notes reviewer per product, and blocks production deploys during posted maintenance.
tradeoffs: Coverage of every integration versus the cost of preview testing
follow_ups: How automated is the preview regression?
Who owns an integration with no named admin?
weak_answer_warnings: Ad hoc 'we will watch production' with no notes or preview step

interview_questions.question: How do you convince a busy team to read the release notes every season?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: I show one past production incident that release notes would have caught, then give them a filtered checklist and a preview-sandbox window instead of asking them to read every page.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: People ignore unread catalogs. I tie notes to the products they own, time the work to the 4–5 week preview window Help describes, and keep API version checks on the same checklist. I admit notes are not exhaustive for every org bug. I never moralize. The business case is cheaper than firefighting after a seasonal production upgrade you cannot delay. If they still refuse, I record the skipped review as a risk on the change calendar.
interview_questions.example: Last Summer a Flow element change was in the notes; the team that skipped them spent a weekend on production incidents the preview sandbox would have shown.
tradeoffs: Hours of filtered reading versus weekend production firefighting
follow_ups: Which products does this team actually use?
Do they have a preview sandbox this cycle?
weak_answer_warnings: Moralizing without a concrete incident or a filtered process
